paper_metadata.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Method for Bank Account Fraud Detection using Quantum Encoding and Quantum Machine Learning

summary: The paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical bank-account fraud detection study using an 8-qubit QSVM with angle encoding on 750 sampled instances per run, evaluated over six runs on a synthetic Feedzai dataset suite with 31 features and six temporal variants. The quantum model underperformed the classical XGBoost baseline, which achieved reported ROC-AUC scores in the 89%–95% range, and the paper does not demonstrate practical quantum advantage.

experiments.description: Hybrid quantum-classical fraud detection using a quantum support vector machine with angle encoding and an eight-qubit quantum kernel, compared against classical XGBoost baselines across six synthetic bank-account fraud dataset variants.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Eight selected features were encoded, with one feature per qubit; categorical data was level-encoded to numerical values before encoding.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Binary classification of bank-account fraud vs non-fraud using a quantum kernel SVM.

problem_instance.description: Bank account fraud detection on a synthetic dataset suite created by Feedzai Research with six temporal variants and induced biases/noise.
problem_instance.dataset_name: Feedzai Research bank account fraud dataset suite

dataset_specification.description: Six temporal variants spanning February to September; 31 features; induced Laplacian noise; missing values; group size disparity, prevalence disparity, and temporal biases; 80/20 train-test split for classical pipeline, but quantum section sampled 750 instances (250 fraud, 500 non-fraud)

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Removed three columns with >25% missing values; removed rows with missing data in remaining columns; removed duplicates and unnecessary information; level-encoded categorical features; scaled feature sets; converted targets to numerical arrays and float types; reduced feature set from 16 to 8 qubits due to computational/time constraints.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Model run six times; evaluated using precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, and accuracy on training and testing sets; compared against XGBoost baseline across dataset variants.

implementation_details.classical_solver: SVM with quantum kernel; classical baseline XGBoost
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Feature selection, missing-value handling, duplicate removal, level encoding, scaling, train-test preparation.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Computed precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, and accuracy; compared quantum and classical KPI scores.

speedup_claims.conditions: Current hardware limitations; hybrid quantum-classical fraud detection on synthetic bank-account fraud datasets
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports the quantum model underperformed the classical baseline and does not claim any speedup or quantum advantage.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: More qubits, larger and cleaner training sets, better quantum kernels/circuits, and substantially improved hardware fidelity would be needed before any advantage could be plausible.
limiting_factors: Quantum model underperformed the classical XGBoost baseline
Only 750 sampled instances per run were used for the quantum experiment
Current hardware limitations and noise constraints
No demonstrated speedup or quantum advantage

notes: The paper explicitly describes a hybrid quantum-classical QSVM using eight qubits and angle encoding, but does not name a specific quantum hardware backend, provider, simulator, circuit depth, shot count, or transpilation details.
Speedup order is inferred as none_proven because the paper reports lower quantum KPI scores than the classical XGBoost baseline and does not claim asymptotic quantum advantage.
The paper reports that the quantum model did not do as well as the classical models and under-performed compared to XGBoost.
The quantum experiment used an 8-qubit QSVM with angle encoding on a sampled 750-instance subset, which is a small-scale NISQ demonstration.
